questions.stem: Human body cells contain 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 pairs. A sperm cell contains 23 chromosomes. What would happen if gametes were not haploid?

options.text: The offspring would be haploid and have only half the normal chromosome number
The chromosome number would double with each generation, leading to cells with abnormal numbers of chromosomes
The offspring would be genetically identical to the mother
Nothing different would happen; the chromosome number would stay at 46

questions.explanation: Meiosis halves the chromosome number to produce haploid gametes (23 chromosomes). At fertilisation, two haploid gametes fuse to restore the diploid number (46). If gametes were diploid (46), the zygote would have 92 chromosomes, and the number would keep doubling each generation. This is why meiosis is essential for sexual reproduction.

questions.stem: A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a specific protein. Where exactly are genes located?

options.text: Floating freely in the cytoplasm of the cell
On chromosomes in the nucleus, at specific positions called loci
In the cell membrane, controlling what enters and leaves the cell
Inside ribosomes, where proteins are made

questions.explanation: Genes are sections of DNA located on chromosomes within the cell nucleus. Each gene has a specific position (locus) on a particular chromosome. Humans have around 20,000-25,000 genes distributed across their 23 pairs of chromosomes. The entire set of genetic material in an organism is called its genome.

questions.stem: Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes. One chromosome in each pair comes from the mother and one from the father. Why is this important for genetic variation?

options.text: It means each child receives exactly the same genes from both parents
It means offspring inherit a unique combination of alleles from each parent, producing variation
It ensures all siblings are genetically identical
It means the child always resembles the mother more than the father

questions.explanation: Each parent contributes one chromosome from each pair via their gametes. Since meiosis shuffles which chromosomes go into which gamete (independent assortment), each gamete carries a unique combination of alleles. At fertilisation, the random combination of one sperm and one egg produces offspring with a unique set of alleles from both parents.

questions.stem: The Human Genome Project mapped all the genes in human DNA. A doctor uses genome data to identify that a patient carries a gene variant linked to increased breast cancer risk. This is an example of:

options.text: Gene therapy, where faulty genes are replaced
Genetic screening, using genome data to predict disease risk
Selective breeding, choosing individuals with desirable traits
Cloning, producing genetically identical copies of organisms

questions.explanation: This is genetic screening - using knowledge of an individual's genome to identify gene variants associated with disease. The Human Genome Project provided the reference sequence that makes such screening possible. It allows personalised medicine, where treatment and monitoring can be tailored to a person's genetic risk factors.

questions.stem: A chromosome is made of a DNA molecule wrapped around histone proteins. What is the advantage of DNA being tightly coiled around proteins in chromosomes?

options.text: It makes DNA easier to replicate during cell division
It allows the very long DNA molecule to fit inside the small nucleus and be organised for accurate distribution during cell division
It prevents mutations from occurring in the DNA
It speeds up protein synthesis by keeping genes close together

questions.explanation: A single human cell contains about 2 metres of DNA, which must fit into a nucleus only about 6 micrometres in diameter. Wrapping DNA around histone proteins and coiling it tightly into chromosomes compacts it enormously. During cell division, this compact form also ensures chromosomes can be accurately separated and distributed to daughter cells.
